opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's mostly about de-risking. When you're setting up something like a Go learning pipeline for the first time, there are a lot of moving parts: the board representation, the network architecture, the search, the self-play loop, the training infrastructure. If you go straight to learning from scratch, the AlphaZero-style tabula rasa approach, and it doesn't work, you have no idea which of those pieces is broken. Your agent is just playing random moves against itself, and the signal you get back is very weak and noisy.

If you first do supervised learning on expert human games, you get a much tighter feedback loop. You have a clear target: can the network predict what a strong human would play in this position? You can measure that accuracy directly, and you know roughly what good numbers look like because people have published them. So it's a sanity check on your whole stack. If your policy network can get to a reasonable move-prediction accuracy, you know your data pipeline, your model, and your training code are basically sound.

Then once you have that, you can bolt on the search and self-play, and you're starting from a policy that already plays coherent Go, so the games it generates are meaningful rather than noise. That's essentially the path the original AlphaGo took before AlphaGo Zero showed you could drop the human data.

The broader principle I believe in is: first get something working, even if it's not the most elegant or general approach, and then strip away the scaffolding. Learning from scratch is the more beautiful result, but it's a harder engineering problem, and it's much easier to attempt once you've already proven the rest of the system works. Human data is a kind of training wheels that lets you debug everything else.

r001.rationale: The response recommends first getting a working system with supervised learning on expert games, then adding search and self-play, instead of starting from scratch.

r002.rationale: It discusses move prediction and noisy self-play signals, but does not explain that outcome training can predict roughly 50% win probability for early positions with evenly split continuations.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it comes down to de-risking. When you're trying to get a learning system off the ground, the thing that kills you isn't the final performance, it's not knowing whether your pipeline works at all. If you start from scratch with pure self-play, and the agent plateaus at some garbage level, you have no idea why. Is it the architecture? Is it the reward being too sparse? Is it exploration? Is there a bug in how you're encoding the board? Every one of those failure modes looks identical from the outside, which is just "it's not learning."

If you initialize from expert human play, you get a supervised signal that's dense and well-understood. You can check your data loader, your network, your training loop, and you know what good looks like. You get a policy that plays plausibly within hours instead of weeks. And now when you flip on reinforcement learning on top of it, you're starting from a place where the agent is already in the interesting part of the game. The random policy in Go basically never stumbles into good positions, so the RL signal early on is close to noise. The human prior gets you past that cold-start problem.

The other thing I'd say is that there's a kind of engineering humility in it. The AlphaGo story is often told as, "and then AlphaGo Zero showed you don't need humans at all," and that's true, but they got there after they'd already built the whole system with human data and knew every component worked. The from-scratch result was impressive precisely because they had the confidence to remove the crutch. If you try to do that on day one, you're combining a research bet with a debugging nightmare, and I think you should decouple those.

So I'm not saying human data is the ceiling. I'm saying it's the scaffolding. Use it to get something working, understand your system, and then take it away once you can tell the difference between "the idea doesn't work" and "I have a bug."

r001.rationale: The response recommends using expert human play to establish and debug a working baseline, then adding reinforcement learning and removing the human-data scaffold once the system is understood.

r002.rationale: It discusses noisy early reinforcement-learning signals, but does not say that outcome training predicts about a 50% win probability for early positions with roughly even win/loss continuations.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with expert human play because it makes the experiment much easier to debug. If you start from scratch and the agent doesn’t learn, you don’t know whether the problem is exploration, the reward signal, the optimization, or a bug in your implementation. There are just a lot of things that have to work simultaneously.

With human games, you can first ask a much simpler question: can this model learn to predict good moves? Once that works, you have a useful starting policy, and you can test whether self-play improves it. You’ve broken a difficult problem into stages where you can actually tell whether you’re making progress.

That doesn’t mean human play should be the ceiling. It’s a bootstrap. Learning from scratch is a fascinating experiment, but I’d want to establish that the rest of the machinery works before taking away that scaffolding.

r001.rationale: The response recommends first training on expert human games to establish a useful starting policy, then testing whether self-play improves it, instead of beginning from scratch.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss predicting approximately 50% win probability for early Go positions with roughly evenly split outcomes.

sol-6.1.text:
Because human play gives you a very useful starting point. If you initialize randomly, you spend a huge amount of compute rediscovering things that humans already know. And early in training, self-play can be a little misleading: you’re getting better at beating an opponent that’s also terrible, which isn’t necessarily the same as making progress toward strong Go.

I’d rather first get the system to imitate expert games, so it has some notion of what reasonable play looks like, and then use reinforcement learning to push beyond that. I don’t think learning from humans necessarily puts a ceiling on the system. It just gives you a better initialization. Learning from scratch is interesting if that’s the scientific question you want to study, but if the goal is to build a strong player efficiently, why throw away that information?

r001.rationale: It recommends first imitating expert games to establish reasonable play, then using reinforcement learning to improve, rather than starting randomly.
